blocks.text: The chapter closes the letter by addressing community leadership, mutual humility, anxiety, vigilance, and suffering. Elders are to care for the flock willingly and as examples rather than dominating it; humility and entrusting anxiety to God lead into the call to watchfulness. The suffering mentioned here is real social hostility, but the letter does not identify a particular ruler or an empire-wide decree behind it.

The final greetings name Silvanus, “Babylon,” and Mark, but the chapter does not fully define their roles or identities. Silvanus may have carried the letter, assisted in its composition, collaborated in some other way, or served as a stylistic intermediary; the wording does not decide among these possibilities. “Babylon” probably refers symbolically to Rome, yet the letter itself never explicitly makes that identification, so a literal Babylon and other proposals remain possible.

The image of the devil as a roaring lion is a vivid comparison for threat, not a license to turn opponents into subhuman agents of Satan or to build conspiracy theories around the passage. Likewise, casting anxiety on God presents divine care amid distress; it should not be used to shame those with anxiety, require emotional suppression, or replace mental-health treatment.

This conclusion belongs to a coherent letter that combines blessing, moral exhortation, interpretation of Scripture, household instruction, and consolation shaped by future hope. Its final summons to stand firm gathers those broader concerns into a closing charge.
